newsitem.title: CANADA: SAA eyes future US-Joburg rate hike.
newsitem.headline: SAA eyes future US-Joburg rate hike.

text.p: The loss of its lone U.S. competitor did not prompt South African Airways to raise its ex-U.S. cargo rates but a strong fourth quarter peak might, SAA cargo manager for the Americas, Clive Langeveldt told Reuters.
World Airways suspended its Newark-Johannesburg service in August after just two months, part of a withdrawal by the carrier from all scheduled passenger services.
World never mounted much of a threat to SAA Cargo, said Langeveldt, but European carriers have applied downward pressure on U.S.-South Africa rates throughout the year.
"They were more competition for us than the direct carrier on the route," he said in a telephone interview from New York.
Rates slid, said Langeveldt, though he declined to say by how much or where SAA Cargo's rates now stand.
"Any adjustments in rates were done more to counteract the marketing efforts of the European carriers," he said.
Citing Atlanta as an example, European carriers have set a spot pricing floor there by charging about $3 per kg for shipping to South Africa.
The same airlines get as little as 50-55 cents per kg for a transatlantic shipment, so chasing South African traffic is an effective yield raising strategy for them, said Langeveldt.

With the onset of the fall peak, demand for space ex-North America is strong. Even this year's sharp depreciation of the rand has not doused South Africa's thirst for U.S. manufactured and high-tech goods, he said.
At the same time, European carriers have less space to South Africa to market in North America in the fourth quarter because of increased demand from European customers, he said.
"I think the volumes of cargo are going to increase (this fall), and who knows, we might be able to adjust our rates slightly upwards," said Langeveldt.
The amount and timing of a rate increase has not been determined, he said.
World's pullback marked the second time in two years that South African Airways' direct competitor between the U.S. and South Africa had suspended service.

Nor is there likely to be a replacement any time soon. World took over the route authority originally granted to USAfrica Airways, which flew six times weekly between Washington, D.C., and Johannesburg during the winter of 1994-95.
After USAfrica suspended operations, World beat Trans World Airlines to take over the route.
TWA says it has no interest today in succeeding World.
As a result, SAA's 10 passenger flights are likely to be the only direct bellyhold cargo service between the US and South Africa this winter.
SAA also operates two Boeing 747 freighter runs weekly from New York.

The New York-Johannesburg non-stop passenger flights operate with severe weight restructions in order to stretch fuel supplies. Langeveldt said SAA Cargo has been able to uplift an average of eight tonnes per flight, and as much as 11-13 tonnes on some occasions when passenger cabins are less than full. -Air Cargo Newsroom Tel +44 171 542 7706 Fax +44 171 542 5017
